Where it began

Graham Thorpe was born on 1 August 1969 in Farnham. He was playing men's cricket for the village side at Wrecclesham by 13, and soon moved up to Farnham in the Surrey Championship. Football pulled at him too: he was a midfielder for England Schools at under-18 level and had a trial at Brentford.

After Weydon School and Farnham College, a contract from Surrey settled the matter. He made his first-class debut for them at 18, in June 1988, against Leicestershire.

The player

Thorpe played 100 Tests for England from 1993 to 2005, making 6,744 runs at 44.66 with 16 hundreds and 39 fifties. He began as he meant to go on. Picked against Australia at Trent Bridge in 1993, he made an unbeaten 114 in his first Test and was named man of the match.

The high points kept coming. In the 1997 Ashes he and Nasser Hussain added 288 at Edgbaston, and England named him their best player of the series. At Lancaster Park in 2002 he reached 200 not out, his highest score, sharing a stand of 281 with Andrew Flintoff. At the Kensington Oval in 2004 his unbeaten 119 was more than half of England's 226, and England went on to their first series win in the Caribbean since 1968. His 100th Test came against Bangladesh in 2005.

What made him special

He could bat whichever way a match needed. Early on he liked to take the attack to the bowlers. Later he became a patient gatherer who played the ball late, with a short backlift and quick wrists, steering it into the gaps rather than hitting it hard. He was thought the side's best player of spin. At Lahore in 2000 he made 118 with only two boundaries, then a record for the fewest in a Test hundred. He was a man for a chase, too, averaging 108.25 when England won batting last.

If there was a gap in his game, it was turning good starts into big scores, and 39 fifties against 16 hundreds tells the story. Lord's also kept its honours board from him. He played more Tests there than anywhere else, and his best was 89.

Away from the middle

Wisden made him one of its Cricketers of the Year after the 1997 season, and he was appointed MBE. He helped Surrey to a good deal of silverware, including the 1999 County Championship, their first since 1971. After his playing days he turned to coaching, first in Australia with New South Wales and then back home with Surrey and England.

He died on 4 August 2024, aged 55.

And finally

Few batters had a better view of history. Thorpe was in the opposing side in 1994 when Brian Lara made 375, and again in 2004 when Lara made 400 not out. He bowled in Tests without ever taking a wicket, but he could always say that his first wicket in first-class cricket was David Gower, leg before.
